notes:
=== File System Credential Hunting with findstr ===
Recursively search configuration files, scripts, and deployment files for embedded credentials.

=== FINDSTR COMMAND VARIANTS ===
Filename-only sweep (fast initial pass):
  findstr /SIM /C:"password" *.xml *.ini *.txt *.config *.cfg
  /S = recursive, /I = case-insensitive, /M = filename only

Show matching lines:
  findstr /SIN /C:"password" *.xml *.ini *.txt *.config

Skip binary files:
  findstr /SPIN /C:"password" *.*
  /P = skip files with non-printable characters

PowerShell equivalent:
  Select-String -Path C:\Users\*.txt -Pattern password
  Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Include *.config,*.xml,*.ini | Select-String -Pattern "password"

=== HIGH-VALUE TARGET LOCATIONS ===
IIS web.config files (database connection strings):
  C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config
  findstr /si password *.config in C:\inetpub

Unattended installation files (plaintext or base64 passwords):
  C:\Windows\Panther\unattend.xml
  C:\Windows\Panther\unattend\unattend.xml
  C:\Windows\system32\sysprep\sysprep.xml
  C:\Windows\system32\sysprep.inf
  C:\Windows\Setup\Scripts\

Application-specific directories:
  C:\scripts\, C:\tools\, C:\backup\ (admin-created script directories)
  Service application directories under Program Files

Chrome dictionary file (user-added passwords to spellcheck):
  C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Custom Dictionary.txt

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
web.config credentials → database access → data exfil or lateral movement via DB server
Unattended install files → local admin password → immediate admin access
Script directories → embedded service account credentials → lateral movement
Snaffler automates this across network shares: .\Snaffler.exe -s -d <domain> -o snaffler.log -v data

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
base64 strings in config files (easily decoded: [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([System.Convert]::FromBase64String("<b64>"))
Password= Password: pwd= pass= patterns in any file type
Connection strings containing User ID= and Password= or UID= PWD=
.sav files in Windows directories (backup registry hive copies)

recommended.note: Check PowerShell history for typed secrets.
Check the registry for stored creds.

name: Credential Hunting - Search Files for Passwords
description: Recursively grep the filesystem for credentials in config, script, and note files, and hunt files by name/extension (.config, .rdp, .vnc, .cred, unattend.xml, web.config).

defense.why_it_works: Windows configuration files, scripts, and logs frequently contain plaintext passwords, API keys, and connection strings. findstr with recursive search across common config file extensions (*.txt, *.ini, *.cfg, *.config, *.xml) quickly identifies files containing password-related strings that were not intended to be user-readable.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. Read permissions on the filesystem (standard user can read most non-protected directories). Knowledge of common credential-containing extensions.
defense.impact: Discovery of plaintext credentials in config files, web.config files, scripts, or backup files, enabling privilege escalation, lateral movement, or service account compromise.
defense.detection: Mass file search with findstr executed by standard user. Unusual read access to web application directories (%WINDIR%\repair, C:\inetpub). Auditd equivalent: file access anomaly on config files.
defense.artifacts: Process log: findstr /SIM /C:password executed by non-admin | File access events on web.config, unattend.xml, or repair SAM
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*findstr.exe" (CommandLine="*password*" OR CommandLine="*/SIM*")
| table _time, Computer, User, CommandLine
defense.elastic_kql: event.code:"1" AND process.name:findstr.exe AND process.command_line:(*password* OR *SIM*)
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "findstr.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("password","/SIM")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.prevention: Never store plaintext credentials in configuration files. Use Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI), Azure Key Vault, or Windows Credential Manager for secrets. Restrict read access to web application config files (web.config should not be world-readable). Rotate credentials if found in config files.
defense.misconfiguration: web.config or application config files contain plaintext database connection strings with passwords. Unattend.xml from Windows deployment left on disk with AutoLogon credentials. Scripts with hardcoded credentials in world-readable locations.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# World-readable web.config with DB password:
# <connectionStrings>
#   <add connectionString='Server=db;User=sa;Password=P@ssw0rd!' />
# </connectionStrings>

# Attacker searches:
findstr /SIM /C:'password' *.txt *.ini *.cfg *.config *.xml
defense.secure_config:
# Use DPAPI or environment variables for secrets
# web.config: encrypt connectionStrings section
aspnet_regiis.exe -pe 'connectionStrings' -app /MyApp

# Set restrictive file ACLs on config files
icacls web.config /inheritance:r /grant 'IIS_IUSRS:(R)' /grant 'SYSTEM:(F)' /grant 'Administrators:(F)'

# Rotate all credentials found during audits
defense.evasion: Copy the credential store (browser Login Data, .kdbx, PSReadline history) and decrypt/crack it OFFLINE rather than running signatured binaries (LaZagne/SharpChrome) on the host; scope searches to likely paths to limit disk I/O; use built-in cmdlets over dropped tools.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for credential dumping artifacts (LSASS access, SAM hive reads, Kerberos anomalies)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Greps the Windows filesystem for credentials in config and script files:
  findstr /S               recurse into subdirectories
  /I                       case-insensitive
  /M                       print only matching filenames
  /C:"password"           the literal string to find
  *.txt *.ini *.cfg *.config *.xml   the file types to scan
Also hunt by name/extension (.rdp, .vnc, unattend.xml, web.config) and reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s for registry-stored secrets.
